result.summary: The poet addresses Apollo (Phoebus), saying that even the swan sings of him by the river Peneus and that the minstrel with his lyre always sings of him first and last. The poet then greets the god and asks for his favour.

scenes.title: Hymn of praise to Phoebus
scenes.summary: The poet praises Apollo as the subject of song for both swan and human minstrel, then greets him and asks for his favour.

place.name: the bank by the river Peneus

characters.name: Phoebus
characters.description: Apollo, god praised in song by swan and minstrel

characters.name: Peneus
characters.description: eddying river where the swan sings

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo, and the hymn's title names him Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of the swan singing to Apollo and the minstrel beginning and ending with him.

analysis.text: The hymn presents Apollo as the god of song, whom nature (the swan) and human poets alike celebrate.
Homeric hymns served as preludes to recitations, and the closing greeting and request for favour is a standard formula of the genre.

legacy.text: The link between swans and Apollo's music fed the later European tradition of the swan song and of swans as poetic birds.

fun_facts.text: This is one of the shortest Homeric Hymns, only five lines long.

language_notes.text: Phoebus is an epithet-name of Apollo, meaning 'bright' or 'radiant'; it is used here as his address.
'Both first and last' means the minstrel begins and ends every performance with Apollo, so the god frames all song.
'Hail' is a formal greeting that closes the hymn's opening, typical of Homeric Hymns' farewell and salutation formulas.

context_notes.text: Apollo is the god of music, poetry, prophecy and healing; the swan was sacred to him, and the lyre was his instrument.
The Peneus is a major river in Thessaly, northern Greece, flowing to the Aegean.
Ancient hymns commonly ended by asking the god's favour, often hoping for success in the poet's own song or contest.

literary_notes.text: The poet speaks directly to Apollo, making the hymn an act of address and worship rather than narration.
Swan and minstrel are set side by side, 'of you... and of you', showing Apollo praised by nature and humanity alike.
The poet casts himself as a humble petitioner, in contrast with the god's grand praise above.
